faq.q: What is the first test for a patient with fever in a low‑resource setting?

faq.a: Look for high WBC with left shift, high CRP, and clinical signs of organ dysfunction.
faq.q: How do you differentiate bacterial sepsis from viral infection?

faq.a: If the patient has no oedema, normal JVP, and a clear chest X‑ray, heart failure is unlikely.
faq.q: When can you safely rule out heart failure?

exam: A 28‑year‑old man presents with fever and rigors. What is the next best step? — Perform a malaria rapid test and a CBC; treat if malaria positive, otherwise consider bacterial sepsis.
A 45‑year‑old woman has pedal oedema and ascites. What is the most likely diagnosis? — Heart failure; confirm with raised JVP and cardiomegaly on chest X‑ray.
A child has a sore throat and low‑grade fever. Which condition must be ruled out first? — Group A streptococcal pharyngitis; perform a rapid strep test.
A patient with chest pain has a normal ECG. What is the next investigation? — Cardiac enzymes (troponin) to rule out myocardial infarction.
A 60‑year‑old presents with jaundice and abdominal pain. What is the priority diagnosis? — Acute hepatitis; check viral hepatitis serology and liver function tests.
A patient with sudden headache and vomiting is found to have a normal CT head. What is the next step? — Consider subarachnoid haemorrhage; repeat CT or perform lumbar puncture if safe.
A 35‑year‑old with cough and weight loss has a normal chest X‑ray. What must be excluded? — Tuberculosis; perform a sputum smear and GeneXpert.
A patient with abdominal pain has a normal ultrasound. Which condition should still be considered? — Acute appendicitis; clinical assessment and possible surgical referral.
ai.title: Must Rule Out Conditions
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: When a patient presents with a common symptom, clinicians must systematically exclude life‑threatening causes before settling on a benign diagnosis. This page outlines the approach, key investigations, and common pitfalls in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: In busy wards, a vague complaint can mask a serious disease. A structured rule‑out list ensures that potentially fatal conditions are not missed, especially where advanced tests are scarce.
A rule‑out list is a diagnostic safety net. It prioritises conditions by prevalence, severity, and treatability, guiding the clinician through history, examination, and affordable investigations.

t.b: If pedal oedema with raised JVP, think heart failure; if ascites with clear fluid, think liver disease; if normal JVP, consider nephrotic syndrome
Malaria smear positive = malaria; WBC >15,000 with left shift = bacterial sepsis; normal counts with rigors = viral

b: Malaria rapid test first for fever
sections.p: In East African hospitals, common life‑threatening mimics include malaria, typhoid, HIV‑associated sepsis, and rheumatic heart disease. Rapid exclusion prevents morbidity and mortality.

b: Ask about travel history for malaria
Look for murmurs in rheumatic heart disease
sections.p: Examiners often ask what you would do next or how you distinguish similar presentations. Focus on the most dangerous differentials first.

b: Failing to check JVP in oedema
sections.p: Assuming a benign cause without ruling out severe disease, over‑reliance on a single test, and neglecting local disease prevalence.
